Introduction

{SPEAKER_DOPPLER}{PART_000}I am Dr. Douglass Doppler, head of materials science for the American Space Agency. It is 5:04am in the early morning of May 13th, 1973. I am joined by the well-respected computer programmer and graphics engineer Dr. Bryan Bautista, the renowned professor of linguistics at Boston College, Dr. Carrie Collins, and astronomer Dr. Alan Akers. In addition, we are joined by a translator— why a translator, I hope you will soon understand.

{SPEAKER_DOPPLER}{PART_000}Forty-six hours and thirty-six minutes ago, a meteor entered our atmosphere and struck the surface of the Earth. It touched down just 20 kilometers north of Alaska's Cape Espenberg. Arctic geoseismic stations detected the impact and alerted the Space Agency.

{SPEAKER_DOPPLER}{PART_000}We begin this thorough investigation because, unlike any rock to enter our atmosphere, this one broadcasts electromagnetic waves. It is embedded with technology similar to human radio towers. Somehow, this foreign radio technology has remained intact, even after a crash landing on our planet's surface. We firmly believe this to be the work of an extraterrestrial intelligent lifeform, a message from deep space.
{SPEAKER_DOPPLER}{PART_000}Now, are there any questions for the team?
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}What signal is it transmitting?
{SPEAKER_DOPPLER}{PART_000}Just 1 singular frequency for roughly 0.8 seconds. It stops for just as long, then resumes.
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}The signal, what frequency?
{SPEAKER_DOPPLER}{PART_000}It's, uh, roughly 1.4 million kilohertz.
{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}YES!! THAT'S WHAT I WAS HOPING YOU'D SAY!
{SPEAKER_DOPPLER}{PART_000}Dr. Akers! Clearly that means something to you. Tell us.

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}It's the Hydrogen Line! Hydrogen atoms, they, when their electron changes spin, they release electromagnetic radiation, and it's at exactly that frequency: 1,402,000 kHz. We detect it all the time in space. That's how we map out galaxies and stars and where matter is, all that jazz, especially since Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the entire universe!
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}How do we know this isn't naturally produced by the meteorite?
{SPEAKER_BAUTISTA}{PART_000}It pauses.

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}Yes! It has regular, periodic, transmissions. Nothing would naturally do that, at least, not so precisely it sounds. And this signal, the Hydrogen Line, it's the perfect thing to broadcast to space.
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}Why is that?

{SPEAKER_AKERS}{PART_000}Because it's the same everywhere. A Hydrogen atom is a Hydrogen atom in this system or any other. You send a meteoroid hurtling across the universe to broadcast the Hydrogen Line— you're telling any intelligent life that hear it that you have something you wanna say.
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}So something is waving hello.
{SPEAKER_BAUTISTA}{PART_000}Or lighting a flare.

{SPEAKER_DOPPLER}{PART_000}And this is exactly why you 4 are here. You are the perfect team for the job. Bautista, take them to the transmission room. Get the team set up on the computer and start broadcasting transmissions.
{SPEAKER_COLLINS}{PART_000}What do we broadcast?
{SPEAKER_DOPPLER}{PART_000}That is up to you. Figure out what it is the aliens want to say. That's your mission.
